Order a bedside transabdominal ultrasound to assess placental location before any intervention.

after.text: Administer uterotonic agents after delivery of the placenta
Proceed with immediate cesarean delivery after rapid maternal stabilization.
Begin massive transfusion protocol before surgical intervention
Perform emergency hysterectomy for presumed uterine rupture

whyEachWrong.a: Uterotonics are given after delivery, not before cesarean
whyEachWrong.c: Stabilization and delivery take precedence over transfusion protocol
whyEachWrong.d: Hysterectomy is for uterine rupture, not abruptio placentae

stem: A 68-year-old man is admitted to the ICU for septic shock secondary to a perforated diverticulitis. He is intubated and placed on vasopressor support. A triple-lumen central venous catheter (CVC) is inserted in the right internal jugular vein using full sterile barrier precautions. On hospital day 4, his temperature rises to 38.9°C (102°F), heart rate is 112/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg on norepinephrine 0.08 µg/kg/min, and white blood cell count is 16,200/mm³ with a left shift. Blood cultures drawn from the CVC grow coagulase‑negative Staphylococcus. Which of the following interventions is MOST effective in preventing a catheter‑related bloodstream infection in this patient moving forward?

before.text: Replace the existing CVC with a new catheter at a different anatomic site using maximal sterile barrier precautions.
Apply chlorhexidine‑impregnated dressings to the catheter insertion site and change dressings every 7 days.
Administer prophylactic systemic antibiotics for 7 days after catheter insertion.
Use heparin lock solution in each lumen when the catheter is not in use.

after.text: Obtain a new central line insertion kit and replace the catheter immediately.
Apply chlorhexidine‑impregnated dressings to the catheter insertion site and change dressings every 7 days.
Increase the norepinephrine infusion rate to maintain MAP above 65 mmHg.
Start intravenous vancomycin therapy for presumed methicillin‑resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection.

whyEachWrong.a: Catheter replacement is not the first step; prevention should precede replacement.
whyEachWrong.c: Hemodynamic support is essential but does not address infection prevention, the priority here.
whyEachWrong.d: Vancomycin targets MRSA, not coagulase‑negative Staphylococcus, which is the organism identified.

stem: A 58-year-old man with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes is admitted for evaluation of worsening shortness of breath. On admission his vitals are BP 158/92 mmHg, HR 112 bpm, RR 24 breaths/min, O2 sat 88% on room air. Labs reveal BNP 820 pg/mL, serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, and a negative troponin. A chest X‑ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. The medical team initiates furosemide IV, orders a CT pulmonary angiogram, and consults cardiology. While reviewing the chart, the nurse notices that the patient’s adult daughter, who lives out of state, has called and asked for the results of the CT scan before it is performed. The nurse knows the patient has not signed a release of information form. According to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), what is the most appropriate action for the nurse to take?

before.text: Provide the daughter with a verbal summary of the patient’s current condition, as family members are allowed to receive health information.
Explain that the patient’s results cannot be disclosed to anyone without a signed authorization and advise the daughter to contact the patient directly.
Tell the daughter that the CT scan will be performed and that the results will be sent to her via email, as electronic communication is permissible under HIPAA.
Ask the physician to call the daughter and give a brief overview of the patient’s condition, since physicians may share information without a release.

after.text: Tell the daughter that the CT results will be shared with her after the physician reviews the images and the patient gives permission.
Explain that the patient’s results cannot be disclosed to anyone without a signed authorization and advise the daughter to contact the patient directly.
Inform the daughter that the CT scan will be performed promptly to rule out a pulmonary embolism, then discuss the results with her.
Explain that the CT scan is unnecessary and suggest a bedside echocardiogram instead.

whyEachWrong.a: Discloses information before the patient authorizes it.
whyEachWrong.c: Addresses diagnostic urgency rather than confidentiality.
whyEachWrong.d: Recommends a different diagnostic test not indicated for the presented condition.

stem: A 68-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation is admitted for a new diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis (DVT). She has a history of hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3 (eGFR 45 mL/min), and a prior intracranial hemorrhage 2 years ago. On admission, her vital signs are BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, RR 16/min, Temp 36.8°C, O2 sat 98% on room air. Labs: hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, platelet count 210 × 10^3/µL, INR 1.0, aPTT 30 seconds, serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL. The emergency department physician initiates a continuous intravenous unfractionated heparin (UFH) infusion at 18 U/kg/h and orders a repeat aPTT in 6 hours. Six hours later, the aPTT is 78 seconds (therapeutic range 60‑80 seconds). The patient reports mild bruising at the infusion site but no bleeding. The next morning, the physician plans to transition the patient to oral anticoagulation for long‑term therapy. Which of the following is the safest next step in managing her anticoagulation?

before.text: Discontinue UFH and start warfarin 5 mg daily without a loading dose, monitoring INR daily
Continue UFH infusion, add low‑dose warfarin (2 mg daily), and obtain INR after 48 hours before stopping UFH
Stop UFH, start therapeutic low‑molecular‑weight heparin (LMWH) at standard dosing, and bridge to warfarin after 5 days
Maintain UFH infusion, obtain a repeat aPTT in 6 hours, and transition directly to a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) once aPTT is therapeutic

after.text: Obtain a repeat aPTT now and adjust the UFH dose before adding low‑dose warfarin.
Continue UFH infusion, add low‑dose warfarin (2 mg daily), and obtain INR after 48 hours before stopping UFH
Start low‑dose warfarin now and plan to discontinue UFH once the INR is therapeutic.
Switch to low‑molecular‑weight heparin and begin oral rivaroxaban for acute pulmonary embolism.

whyEachWrong.a: The aPTT has already been obtained; repeating it now is unnecessary and delays therapy.
whyEachWrong.c: Initiating warfarin before confirming stable UFH therapy is not the immediate safety priority.
whyEachWrong.d: The management described is appropriate for pulmonary embolism, not for isolated DVT.

stem: A 68‑year‑old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is admitted for acute decompensated heart failure. Her home regimen includes insulin glargine 20 U subcutaneously nightly and insulin lispro 10 U before each meal. On admission, her blood glucose is 212 mg/dL, serum potassium is 3.2 mmol/L, and her creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL (eGFR 35 mL/min). The physician orders a basal‑bolus insulin regimen: insulin glargine 15 U SC at 2200 h, insulin lispro 5 U before each meal, and a correctional insulin lispro scale of 1 U for every 30 mg/dL glucose above 180 mg/dL. The nurse is preparing the insulin lispro for the 0700 h breakfast dose. Which action is the most appropriate to ensure insulin administration safety for this patient?

before.text: Administer the insulin lispro dose from the original vial without checking the expiration date because it is a short‑acting insulin.
Verify the patient’s serum potassium level and hold the scheduled lispro dose until potassium is >3.5 mmol/L.
Calculate the correctional dose based on the current glucose of 212 mg/dL and add it to the scheduled 5 U lispro dose.
Dilute the lispro dose with normal saline to reduce the risk of dosing error.

after.text: Administer the scheduled lispro dose at 0700 h, then check the potassium level afterward.
Verify the patient’s serum potassium level and hold the scheduled lispro dose until potassium is >3.5 mmol/L.
Check the patient's blood glucose and give a correctional lispro dose before the scheduled breakfast dose.
Hold the lispro dose and give an oral potassium supplement because the patient has renal failure.

whyEachWrong.a: The insulin should not be given before confirming potassium is safe; timing is incorrect.
whyEachWrong.c: Addressing hyperglycemia before correcting the low potassium is not the safety priority.
whyEachWrong.d: Potassium replacement is appropriate for hypokalemia, not for renal failure; the condition is wrong.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her partner after a suicide attempt by ingesting 30 tablets of 5 mg clonazepam. She is alert, oriented, and cooperative. Vitals: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 96/min, RR 18/min, Temp 37.0°C, SpO2 99% on room air. Laboratory results show: serum Clonazepam level 12 µg/mL (therapeutic 2-20 µg/mL), serum electrolytes, glucose, and CBC are within normal limits. The patient reports feeling "hopeless" and says, "I don't see a reason to live," but denies a specific plan to kill herself again. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next step in her suicide risk assessment?

before.text: Ask the patient to complete a written Beck Hopelessness Scale before discharge.
Conduct a focused assessment of suicidal ideation, intent, and plan, including asking about access to means.
Schedule a follow‑up appointment with her outpatient psychiatrist within two weeks.
Initiate a brief cognitive‑behavioral therapy session in the ED before discharge.

after.text: Administer IV flumazenil now to reverse the clonazepam effect before evaluating suicide risk.
Conduct a focused assessment of suicidal ideation, intent, and plan, including asking about access to means.
Obtain a serum electrolyte panel and cardiac enzymes to rule out metabolic causes of depression.
Begin treatment with sertraline for major depressive disorder before assessing current suicidal thoughts.

whyEachWrong.a: Reversal of sedation is not indicated; the patient is alert and the focus should be on assessing ideation first.
whyEachWrong.c: Laboratory tests are not the priority; immediate suicide risk assessment supersedes routine labs.
whyEachWrong.d: Sertraline treats depression, not acute benzodiazepine overdose; the scenario requires assessment of current suicidal intent.

stem: A 68-year-old male with a history of severe COPD, hypertension, and recent ischemic stroke is admitted to the medical-surgical unit for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure. On admission his vital signs are: BP 158/92 mmHg, HR 112 bpm, RR 28 breaths/min, SpO2 88% on 2 L nasal cannula, Temp 37.2°C. ABG shows pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 68 mmHg, PaO₂ 58 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 28 mEq/L. He is placed on BiPAP with settings of IPAP 18 cm H₂O and EPAP 8 cm H₂O. Over the next hour his mental status deteriorates: he becomes agitated, attempts to remove the BiPAP mask, and is pulling at his IV lines. The nurse assesses that the patient is at risk for self-harm and respiratory compromise. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action to ensure restraint safety while maintaining the patient's respiratory status?

before.text: Apply a soft wrist restraint and continue BiPAP without further assessment.
Stop BiPAP, place the patient in a supine position, and apply a full‑body mitt restraint.
Reassess the patient's airway, breathing, and oxygenation, then apply a soft mitt restraint while maintaining BiPAP.
Increase the BiPAP pressure settings to reduce agitation, then apply a hip‑level restraint.

after.text: First, reassess the patient's airway, breathing, and oxygenation, then consider applying a soft mitt restraint.
Increase the BiPAP pressure settings to improve ventilation before addressing the restraint need.
Reassess the patient's airway, breathing, and oxygenation, then apply a soft mitt restraint while maintaining BiPAP.
Apply a hard wrist restraint to prevent line removal for a patient with suspected seizures.

whyEachWrong.a: Restraint should not be applied before confirming airway and breathing stability.
whyEachWrong.b: Ventilator adjustments are not the immediate priority when the patient is at risk of self‑harm.
whyEachWrong.d: Hard wrist restraints are for seizure activity, not for a hypercapnic respiratory failure patient.

stem: A 68‑year‑old woman with a history of chronic kidney disease stage 4 is undergoing elective total hip arthroplasty. She receives 2 units of leukoreduced packed red blood cells intraoperatively. Twenty minutes after the second unit is started, she develops fever of 38.9°C (102°F), chills, diffuse erythema, and a sudden drop in blood pressure to 85/50 mmHg. Her heart rate is 115/min, respiratory rate 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL (pre‑transfusion 8.5 g/dL) and a serum bilirubin of 1.2 mg/dL (baseline 0.8 mg/dL). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

before.text: Administer intravenous antihistamine and continue the transfusion at a slower rate
Immediately stop the transfusion, maintain the IV line with normal saline, and obtain blood cultures
Give intravenous methylprednisolone and resume the transfusion after a 30‑minute observation period
Order a repeat cross‑match and re‑infuse the remaining portion of the same blood unit

after.text: Pause the transfusion, then administer antihistamine and monitor vital signs
Immediately stop the transfusion, maintain the IV line with normal saline, and obtain blood cultures
Give intravenous epinephrine bolus and then resume the transfusion after stabilization
Start a rapid infusion of packed red blood cells to treat suspected hemolytic anemia

whyEachWrong.a: Action is appropriate for a transfusion reaction but should be done after stopping the transfusion, not before.
whyEachWrong.c: Epinephrine is not the first priority; stopping the transfusion and obtaining cultures precede pharmacologic intervention.
whyEachWrong.d: Hemolytic anemia requires different management; the scenario describes an acute transfusion reaction.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is admitted to the medical‑surgical unit with a new diagnosis of stage II colon cancer. Her attending physician orders a colonoscopy and a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis. While reviewing the electronic health record (EHR), the nurse notices that the patient’s chart contains a note from a previous psychiatric admission that is not relevant to the current hospitalization. The patient’s daughter, who is visiting, asks the nurse, "Can you tell me what the note says?" The nurse knows the patient has not given permission for any family members to access her mental health information. Which action is most consistent with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) regarding patient confidentiality?

before.text: Explain to the daughter that all information in the chart is shared with family members unless the patient objects.
Inform the daughter that the psychiatric note is protected health information and cannot be disclosed without the patient’s written authorization.
Tell the daughter the content of the note but advise her to keep it confidential.
Ask the attending physician to remove the psychiatric note from the EHR to prevent accidental disclosure.

after.text: Explain to the daughter that the psychiatric note can be shared now, but will be documented later in the patient's chart.
Inform the daughter that the psychiatric note is protected health information and cannot be disclosed without the patient’s written authorization.
Tell the daughter that you will arrange a family meeting to discuss the overall treatment plan, including the psychiatric note.
Inform the daughter that the note pertains to a previous cardiac condition and can be disclosed without the patient’s consent.

whyEachWrong.a: Discloses protected information before proper authorization – violates HIPAA timing principle.
whyEachWrong.c: Addresses overall care planning rather than the specific confidentiality issue – not the priority action.
whyEachWrong.d: Misidentifies the note’s content as cardiac instead of psychiatric – applies to the wrong condition.

stem: A 28‑year‑old G1P0 woman at 38 weeks' gestation is brought to the labor and delivery unit after a sudden gush of fluid during a routine vaginal exam. She reports feeling a sharp, stabbing pain in her lower abdomen and a sudden loss of fetal movement. Her vitals are: BP 112/68 mmHg, HR 102 bpm, RR 18/min, Temp 37.0°C, O2 sat 98% on room air. The fetal heart rate monitor shows a baseline of 70 bpm with recurrent late decelerations. The cervix is 5 cm dilated, 80% effaced, and the presenting part is not palpable. On gentle palpation, a cord-like structure is felt moving with each uterine contraction. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management step?

before.text: Administer a rapid infusion of 1 L normal saline and prepare for emergent cesarean delivery.
Elevate the presenting fetal head with manual elevation and prepare for emergent cesarean delivery.
Perform an amnioinfusion through a transcervical catheter to increase amniotic fluid volume.
Apply gentle traction on the umbilical cord to deliver the fetus vaginally.

after.text: Administer oxytocin infusion to augment labor and improve uterine contractions
Elevate the presenting fetal head with manual elevation and prepare for emergent cesarean delivery.
Apply continuous fetal scalp electrode monitoring to obtain a more accurate heart rate tracing
Perform immediate amnioinfusion to relieve cord compression and improve fetal oxygenation

whyEachWrong.a: Intervention is for labor progression, not for emergent cord prolapse
whyEachWrong.c: Monitoring does not address the immediate threat to fetal life
whyEachWrong.d: Amnioinfusion treats variable decelerations, not a prolapsed cord

stem: A 68-year-old man with newly diagnosed stage IIIB non–small cell lung carcinoma is scheduled for a video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) lobectomy. Pre‑operative labs show: hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelets 210,000/µL, INR 1.1, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and arterial blood gas on room air: pH 7.44, PaO2 78 mmHg, PaCO2 38 mmHg. The surgeon explains the procedure, its benefits, alternatives (including stereotactic body radiation therapy), and risks (including prolonged air leak, postoperative pneumonia, and 2% mortality). The patient asks if he can consent to the surgery but decline the postoperative epidural analgesia. Which of the following actions is the most appropriate response by the nurse practitioner obtaining informed consent?

before.text: Explain that the epidural is optional, but refusing it may increase postoperative pain and delay recovery, and document his refusal if he insists.
Inform the patient that epidural analgesia is considered part of the surgical plan and cannot be separated from the consent for the lobectomy.
Tell the patient that the epidural can be declined, but the surgeon must be notified and the consent form must be amended to reflect the change.
Advise the patient that refusing the epidural will void the consent for surgery, and the procedure must be postponed until he agrees to all components.

after.text: Tell the patient that the epidural can be declined, but postpone notifying the surgeon and amending the consent form until after the surgery is completed.
Review the patient's laboratory values and correct the hemoglobin level before addressing the epidural request, as optimizing labs is the primary concern.
Tell the patient that the epidural can be declined, but the surgeon must be notified and the consent form must be amended to reflect the change.
Explain that the epidural is unnecessary because the patient's condition is a tension pneumothorax requiring immediate chest tube placement rather than analgesia.

whyEachWrong.a: The response delays surgeon notification and consent amendment, which should occur immediately after the patient’s decision.
whyEachWrong.b: Addressing lab values is not the priority; the consent issue must be resolved before any lab review.
whyEachWrong.d: It treats the patient as having a tension pneumothorax, a different diagnosis unrelated to the consent scenario.

stem: A 45‑year‑old woman with a history of Graves disease treated with radioactive iodine 3 months ago presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of high fever, severe agitation, and palpitations. On exam, her temperature is 40.2°C (104.4°F), heart rate is 150/min, blood pressure is 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate is 28/min, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. She is sweating profusely and has a fine tremor of the outstretched hands. Laboratory results show: TSH <0.01 µIU/mL (reference 0.4–4.0), free T4 6.5 ng/dL (reference 0.8–1.8), total T3 300 ng/dL (reference 80–180), serum potassium 3.2 mEq/L, glucose 180 mg/dL, and arterial blood gas: pH 7.48, PaCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3‑ 22 mEq/L. The patient is given a dose of intravenous propranolol, but her heart rate remains >130/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

before.text: Administer intravenous potassium chloride to correct the hypokalemia before any further therapy.
Begin an intravenous infusion of a thionamide (e.g., propylthiouracil) and give a loading dose of inorganic iodide.
Start a continuous infusion of high‑dose glucocorticoids (e.g., hydrocortisone) without adding any antithyroid medication.
Proceed with emergent synchronized cardioversion to control the tachyarrhythmia.

after.text: Administer oral propranolol now, then reassess the heart rate later.
Begin an intravenous infusion of a thionamide (e.g., propylthiouracil) and give a loading dose of inorganic iodide.
Give intravenous hydrocortisone to reduce peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
Start an intravenous infusion of dopamine to support blood pressure in suspected septic shock.

whyEachWrong.a: Propranolol should be given intravenously first; oral dosing is later in the sequence.
whyEachWrong.c: Hydrocortisone is appropriate for thyroid storm but not the immediate priority after beta‑blockade failure.
whyEachWrong.d: Dopamine treats septic shock, not thyroid storm; the diagnosis is different.

stem: A 62‑year‑old man with metastatic colon cancer is admitted to the ICU for septic shock secondary to a perforated diverticulum. A triple‑lumen right internal jugular central venous catheter (CVC) is placed emergently. His initial vitals are: temperature 38.9°C (102°F), heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg (on norepinephrine 0.12 µg/kg/min), respiratory rate 22/min, SpO₂ 94% on 2 L/min O₂. Laboratory values: WBC 16,800/mm³, serum glucose 210 mg/dL, serum albumin 2.8 g/dL. The ICU team implements a CLABSI prevention bundle that includes daily chlorhexidine bathing, maximal sterile barrier precautions during insertion, and antimicrobial-impregnated dressings. On hospital day 5, the patient’s temperature rises to 39.4°C (103°F), his white count increases to 19,500/mm³, and the catheter site shows mild erythema without purulence. Blood cultures drawn from the CVC and a peripheral vein both grow coagulase‑negative Staphylococcus species within 24 hours. Which of the following interventions is most appropriate to reduce the risk of further central line–associated bloodstream infections in this patient?

before.text: Replace the existing central line with a new catheter at a different anatomic site using maximal sterile barrier precautions
Remove the colonized catheter promptly and initiate targeted antimicrobial therapy
Add a systemic antifungal agent to the current antibiotic regimen
Increase the frequency of chlorhexidine bathing from daily to twice daily

after.text: Obtain a repeat blood culture before changing the catheter
Remove the colonized catheter promptly and initiate targeted antimicrobial therapy
Increase the norepinephrine infusion to improve perfusion
Start empiric antifungal therapy for suspected candidemia

whyEachWrong.a: The catheter should be removed immediately; delaying removal is incorrect
whyEachWrong.c: Hemodynamic support is not the priority for preventing CLABSI
whyEachWrong.d: Antifungal therapy addresses a different infection type

stem: A 68‑year‑old man with metastatic lung cancer is receiving home hospice care. His current medication regimen includes fentanyl transdermal patch (100 mcg/hr) and oral oxycodone 10 mg every 4 hours as needed for breakthrough pain. Yesterday, his family called the nurse because he was difficult to arouse. On arrival, the nurse finds the patient with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 9 (E4 V2 M3), respiratory rate 6 breaths/min, SpO₂ 84% on room air, and a capillary refill of >4 seconds. His arterial blood gas shows pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 58 mmHg, PaO₂ 58 mmHg on 2 L/min nasal cannula. The nurse suspects opioid oversedation. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

before.text: Increase the oxygen flow to 6 L/min via nasal cannula and re‑assess in 15 minutes.
Administer 0.4 mg of naloxone intravenously while continuing to monitor respiratory status.
Discontinue the fentanyl patch and replace it with a lower‑dose patch.
Perform rapid sequence intubation and mechanical ventilation before giving any reversal agent.

after.text: Increase the fentanyl patch dose to 150 mcg/hr after confirming the low GCS score.
Administer 0.4 mg of naloxone intravenously while continuing to monitor respiratory status.
Apply supplemental oxygen via face mask to raise SpO₂ above 90% before any medication changes.
Administer 0.4 mg of naloxone intravenously for suspected severe hypoglycemia.

whyEachWrong.a: Naloxone should be given first; adjusting the fentanyl dose is delayed intervention.
whyEachWrong.c: Oxygen is important but addressing opioid oversedation with naloxone is the priority.
whyEachWrong.d: Naloxone treats opioid overdose, not hypoglycemia; the condition described is opioid oversedation.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with a history of Graves disease treated with radioactive iodine 3 months ago presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of agitation, profuse sweating, and palpitations. She reports that she has been increasingly anxious and unable to sleep for the past 24 hours. Vital signs are: temperature 40.2°C (104.4°F), heart rate 138/min, blood pressure 165/95 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical exam reveals a fine tremor of the outstretched hands, moist skin, and mild exophthalmos. Laboratory results show: TSH 0.02 µIU/mL (reference 0.4–4.0), free T4 5.2 ng/dL (reference 0.8–1.8), and total T3 350 ng/dL (reference 80–180). ECG shows sinus tachycardia with occasional premature ventricular contractions. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

before.text: Administer intravenous propranolol 1 mg every 5 minutes, up to a total dose of 5 mg, and initiate aggressive cooling with ice packs.
Give intravenous propylthiouracil (PTU) 250 mg, followed by a continuous infusion of 50 mg/hour, and start supportive measures including cooling and beta‑blockade.
Start intravenous levothyroxine 200 µg bolus and begin high‑dose corticosteroids.
Begin oral methimazole 30 mg daily and arrange for emergent thyroidectomy within the next 24 hours.

after.text: Administer intravenous propranolol 1 mg, then start cooling measures and give PTU infusion later.
Give intravenous propylthiouracil (PTU) 250 mg, followed by a continuous infusion of 50 mg/hour, and start supportive measures including cooling and beta‑blockade.
Begin aggressive cooling with ice packs and antipyretics, then give PTU infusion and beta‑blockade.
Give intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, then start PTU infusion and beta‑blockade.

whyEachWrong.a: PTU should be given first; the beta‑blocker is delayed incorrectly.
whyEachWrong.c: Cooling is not the immediate priority before controlling thyroid hormone excess.
whyEachWrong.d: Hydrocortisone treats adrenal crisis, not thyroid storm.

stem: A 27-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents to the emergency department after vomiting for 8 hours. She reports feeling extremely thirsty, having abdominal pain, and noticing fruity breath. Her last insulin dose was missed 24 hours ago. Vitals: BP 102/64 mmHg, HR 118 bpm, RR 28/min, Temp 37.8°C, SpO2 98% on room air. Physical exam reveals dry mucous membranes and Kussmaul respirations. Laboratory results: Serum glucose 540 mg/dL, Na 132 mEq/L, K 5.2 mEq/L, Cl 98 mEq/L, BUN 28 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, Arterial pH 7.12, HCO3- 10 mEq/L, Anion gap 24 mEq/L, Serum β‑hydroxybutyrate 5.0 mmol/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management step?

before.text: Begin an intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour without a fluid bolus
Administer 1 L of 0.9% normal saline bolus, then start an insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour
Give 20 mEq of intravenous potassium chloride before starting insulin
Start an intravenous insulin infusion and add 5% dextrose to the fluid when glucose reaches 250 mg/dL

after.text: Begin continuous cardiac monitoring, then obtain a stat serum electrolyte panel before any fluids
Administer 1 L of 0.9% normal saline bolus, then start an insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour
Administer 0.5 mg subcutaneous glucagon immediately, then reassess glucose after 15 minutes
Give 1 L of 0.45% saline, then start a thiamine infusion for suspected Wernicke encephalopathy

whyEachWrong.a: Cardiac monitoring is appropriate later; initial step should be fluid resuscitation
whyEachWrong.c: Glucagon is for hypoglycemia, not the priority in DKA management
whyEachWrong.d: Thiamine and hypotonic saline address Wernicke encephalopathy, not DKA

stem: Mrs. Alvarez, an 82‑year‑old woman with a recent diagnosis of congestive heart failure (CHF) and stage 2 pressure injury on her sacrum, is admitted to the medical‑surgical unit. Her vitals are BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, RR 18/min, SpO2 95% on 2 L nasal cannula, and temperature 37.0°C. Labs show serum albumin 2.9 g/dL, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, and creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. The nurse plans a comprehensive fall and pressure injury prevention strategy. Which of the following interventions should be prioritized to most effectively reduce Mrs. Alvarez's risk for both falls and pressure injury progression during the next 24 hours?

before.text: Apply a low‑profile, pressure‑reducing mattress overlay and encourage the patient to remain in a supine position throughout the shift.
Implement hourly repositioning with a draw‑sheet turn, provide a bedside commode, and ensure the call light is within arm's reach.
Place the patient in a chair with a built‑in seat cushion and schedule a physical therapy gait training session in the afternoon.
Increase protein intake to 1.5 g/kg/day and administer a daily vitamin D supplement to promote wound healing.

after.text: Apply a scheduled medication round before repositioning, then assess pain later in the shift.
Implement hourly repositioning with a draw‑sheet turn, provide a bedside commode, and ensure the call light is within arm's reach.
Place a pressure‑relieving mattress and encourage deep breathing exercises to improve oxygenation.
Administer diuretics and monitor daily weights to manage fluid overload associated with heart failure.

whyEachWrong.a: Intervention is performed before the needed repositioning, delaying fall/pressure injury prevention.
whyEachWrong.c: While beneficial, it does not address the immediate priority of fall and pressure injury risk.
whyEachWrong.d: Focuses on heart failure management, not directly related to fall or pressure injury prevention.

stem: A 68‑year‑old man with acute myeloid leukemia is receiving induction chemotherapy. On hospital day 4, he is transfused with one unit of ABO‑identical, cross‑matched packed red blood cells (PRBCs) at 10:15 AM. At 10:45 AM, he develops sudden onset dyspnea, fever of 38.9°C (102°F), hypotension (BP 88/52 mmHg), tachycardia (HR 118/min), and a diffuse erythematous rash. His oxygen saturation is 84% on room air. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL (pre‑transfusion 7.8 g/dL), a serum lactate of 4.2 mmol/L, and a positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT) with anti‑IgG and anti‑C3. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

before.text: Administer 1 mg intramuscular epinephrine and start continuous cardiac monitoring
Immediately discontinue the transfusion, place the patient in the supine position, and begin aggressive intravenous crystalloid resuscitation
Order a repeat cross‑match and re‑infuse the remaining PRBC unit at a slower rate
Give 1 g intravenous methylprednisolone and observe for symptom resolution

after.text: Cease the transfusion, then begin aggressive intravenous crystalloid resuscitation before repositioning the patient
Immediately discontinue the transfusion, place the patient in the supine position, and begin aggressive intravenous crystalloid resuscitation
Administer intravenous antihistamine and corticosteroid while continuing the transfusion
Discontinue the transfusion, place the patient supine, and start treatment for sepsis with broad‑spectrum antibiotics

whyEachWrong.a: The order is incorrect; the patient should be positioned supine prior to initiating resuscitation
whyEachWrong.c: Treats the reaction but does not address the immediate life‑threatening circulatory collapse
whyEachWrong.d: Targets sepsis rather than transfusion reaction, addressing the wrong diagnosis

stem: A 68‑year‑old man with a history of atrial fibrillation is admitted for acute ischemic stroke. On admission his vital signs are BP 158/92 mmHg, HR 112 bpm, RR 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, and temperature 37.2°C. Labs show: Na 138 mEq/L, K 4.2 mEq/L, Cr 1.1 mg/dL, INR 1.1, and troponin I 0.02 ng/mL. CT brain shows a right middle‑cerebral‑artery infarct. The attending orders tissue‑type plasminogen activator (tPA) and a full stroke work‑up. The patient’s daughter, who lives out of state, calls the nurse and asks for a detailed update on his condition, including the exact time of symptom onset and the planned tPA administration. The nurse considers whether to provide this information. Which of the following actions is most consistent with HIPAA regulations and professional standards of confidentiality?

before.text: Provide the daughter with the full details because the patient is incapacitated and she is his next of kin.
Ask the patient’s legal health care proxy for permission before disclosing any specific clinical information to the daughter.
Disclose only the general diagnosis (stroke) and avoid any specifics, as the patient has not yet signed a release of information.
Refuse to share any information with the daughter, citing the patient’s right to privacy, even if she later provides a signed release.

after.text: Document the patient's vital signs and labs now, then discuss the tPA plan later with the healthcare team.
Ask the patient’s legal health care proxy for permission before disclosing any specific clinical information to the daughter.
Explain the tPA administration schedule to the daughter before confirming the patient's consent for the procedure.
Inform the daughter that the patient’s chest pain suggests a myocardial infarction and that cardiology will be consulted.

whyEachWrong.a: The nurse should first address immediate clinical priorities before providing a detailed update.
whyEachWrong.c: Providing the tPA schedule is not the primary safety concern before confirming consent.
whyEachWrong.d: Chest pain and MI are not part of the presented stroke scenario.

stem: A 68-year-old man is admitted to the medical floor after a 7‑day course of clindamycin for a dental abscess. On hospital day 3 he develops watery diarrhea (7 stools in 24 hours) and mild abdominal cramping. Vital signs: T 38.2°C, HR 102 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 18/min, O2 sat 97% on room air. Laboratory results show WBC 14,000/µL with 85% neutrophils, serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL). A stool assay returns positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin B. The infection control team is called to implement appropriate isolation precautions. Which of the following actions is the most critical component of contact precautions to prevent transmission of C. diff in this patient’s room?

before.text: Place the patient in a private room with a dedicated bathroom and post a sign indicating “Contact Precautions – C. diff.”
Require all healthcare personnel and visitors to don gloves and a gown before entering the patient’s room, and to perform hand hygiene with soap and water after patient contact.
Use alcohol‑based hand sanitizer (ABHS) for hand hygiene before and after patient contact, as it is more convenient than soap and water.
Disinfect the patient’s bedside table and bedside rail with a quaternary ammonium compound after each patient encounter.

after.text: Place the patient on contact precautions after confirming the C. difficile diagnosis, then initiate isolation measures later in the care sequence.
Require all healthcare personnel and visitors to don gloves and a gown before entering the patient’s room, and to perform hand hygiene with soap and water after patient contact.
Provide the patient with a private bathroom and ensure environmental cleaning with sporicidal agents, but prioritize these after initiating antimicrobial therapy.
Require all staff to wear N95 respirators and implement airborne isolation, as would be appropriate for a patient with active tuberculosis.

whyEachWrong.a: Isolation must be instituted immediately; delaying it allows transmission.
whyEachWrong.c: Environmental cleaning is important but not the most critical first step; hand hygiene and PPE are priority.
whyEachWrong.d: N95 respirators and airborne precautions are for TB, not C. difficile.

stem: A 68-year-old man with hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3, and newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation is admitted for rate control and anticoagulation. His vitals are BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 112 bpm, RR 18/min, O2 sat 96% on room air. Labs show: serum creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (eGFR 45 mL/min), INR 1.1, hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL. The physician recommends initiating a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) for stroke prevention and orders a transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) to evaluate for left atrial thrombus before cardioversion. The patient asks, "What are the risks of the medication and the TEE, and do I have to sign a consent?" Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the nurse to ensure informed consent is obtained ethically and legally?

before.text: Explain the benefits of the DOAC, obtain a verbal consent for the medication, and tell the patient that a written signature is not required for the TEE.
Describe the risks, benefits, and alternatives of both the DOAC and the TEE, answer the patient’s questions, and obtain a written signature for each procedure before they are performed.
Tell the patient that the DOAC is safer than warfarin and that the TEE is a routine test, then proceed with the orders without a formal consent.
Ask the physician to obtain consent for the DOAC only, since the TEE is considered a diagnostic test and does not require separate consent.

after.text: Explain the risks, benefits, and alternatives of both the DOAC and the TEE, answer the patient’s questions, and obtain a written signature after the procedures are completed.
Describe the risks, benefits, and alternatives of both the DOAC and the TEE, answer the patient’s questions, and obtain a written signature for each procedure before they are performed.
Begin the TEE immediately, then discuss the DOAC risks later, and obtain consent for the TEE only.
Describe the risks, benefits, and alternatives of warfarin therapy and a cardiac stress test, answer the patient’s questions, and obtain a written signature for each.

whyEachWrong.a: Consent must be obtained before the procedures, not after.
whyEachWrong.c: Addressing the TEE first neglects the immediate need for anticoagulation and does not prioritize stroke prevention.
whyEachWrong.d: The interventions described (warfarin and stress test) do not match the patient’s diagnosis and prescribed DOAC.

stem: Ms. Patel, a 68-year-old woman with COPD exacerbation, is receiving nebulized albuterol and ipratropium, supplemental O₂ at 2 L/min via nasal cannula, and a scheduled dose of IV methylprednisolone 125 mg. Her vitals are: BP 138/84 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, RR 22 breaths/min, SpO₂ 92% on current O₂. The charge RN receives a new order to obtain a stat arterial blood gas (ABG) and to increase the O₂ flow to 4 L/min if the PaO₂ is <60 mmHg. The RN must delegate the ABG collection to a staff member. Which of the following is the most appropriate delegation decision?

before.text: Delegate the ABG collection to a certified nursing assistant (CNA) because the task is routine and does not require professional judgment.
Delegate the ABG collection to a licensed practical nurse (LPN) who has demonstrated competence in arterial puncture and can notify the RN of the results.
Perform the ABG yourself because the RN is the only provider allowed to collect arterial samples in a critical care setting.
Delegate the ABG collection to a patient care technician (PCT) and instruct them to adjust the O₂ flow based on the ABG values.

after.text: Delegate the ABG collection to the LPN after completing the medication administration, which is not the optimal sequence for this urgent need.
Delegate the ABG collection to a licensed practical nurse (LPN) who has demonstrated competence in arterial puncture and can notify the RN of the results.
Delegate the ABG collection to the LPN, but prioritize initiating a rapid response for potential respiratory distress first.
Delegate the ABG collection to the LPN, assuming the patient has a myocardial infarction rather than COPD exacerbation.

whyEachWrong.a: The LPN should collect the ABG immediately, not after other tasks.
whyEachWrong.c: Respiratory assessment takes precedence over delegating the ABG.
whyEachWrong.d: The management described applies to cardiac ischemia, not COPD.

stem: A 68‑year‑old man with a history of cirrhosis secondary to hepatitis C presents to the emergency department after a syncopal episode. He reports 2 days of melena and increasing fatigue. On arrival his blood pressure is 88/52 mmHg, heart rate 124/min, respiratory rate 22/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Physical exam reveals cool, clammy skin, a distended abdomen with shifting dullness, and a faint, non‑pulsatile abdominal bruit. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, Hematocrit 21%, BUN 38 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, INR 1.9, serum lactate 4.2 mmol/L. An emergent upper endoscopy is ordered but not yet performed. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

before.text: Begin intravenous bolus of 1 L normal saline followed by rapid infusion of packed red blood cells (PRBCs) to target a hemoglobin of 10 g/dL
Administer intravenous octreotide infusion, start a norepinephrine drip to maintain MAP >65 mmHg, and transfuse PRBCs to maintain hemoglobin 7‑8 g/dL
Give 2 units of fresh frozen plasma (FFP) before any blood product, and initiate a vasopressin infusion to improve splanchnic perfusion
Perform emergent transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) prior to endoscopic therapy

after.text: Begin immediate blood transfusion to raise hemoglobin above 10 g/dL before any vasoactive support or octreotide infusion
Administer intravenous octreotide infusion, start a norepinephrine drip to maintain MAP >65 mmHg, and transfuse PRBCs to maintain hemoglobin 7‑8 g/dL
Administer intravenous pantoprazole, initiate a norepinephrine drip to keep MAP >65 mmHg, and give PRBCs to maintain hemoglobin 7‑8 g/dL
Administer intravenous terlipressin, initiate a dopamine infusion to sustain MAP >65 mmHg, and give PRBCs to maintain hemoglobin 7‑8 g/dL

whyEachWrong.a: Intervention should follow hemodynamic stabilization; transfusing to a higher hemoglobin target first is premature
whyEachWrong.c: Octreotide, not pantoprazole, is the priority pharmacologic therapy for variceal bleeding
whyEachWrong.d: Terlipressin is used for hepatorenal syndrome, not acute variceal hemorrhage

stem: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is admitted for a left total knee arthroplasty. His home regimen includes insulin glargine 20 units SC nightly and insulin lispro 5 units SC with meals. Postoperatively, his orders are: insulin glargine 20 units SC at 2100, insulin lispro 4 units IV push before each meal, and a sliding scale of regular insulin (0.05 U/kg) for glucose >180 mg/dL. At 0800, his capillary glucose is 212 mg/dL. The nurse prepares a dose of regular insulin 4 units IV push. Before administration, she notices the insulin vial is labeled "Regular Insulin 100 U/mL" and the syringe she is using is a 1‑mL tuberculin (U‑100) syringe. Which action should the nurse take to ensure safe insulin administration?

before.text: Administer the 4‑unit dose as drawn, because the syringe is calibrated for U‑100 insulin.
Recalculate the dose using the concentration of the insulin vial and draw the correct volume in the tuberculin syringe.
Switch to a 0.5‑mL insulin syringe and administer 4 units, as the dose is low.
Ask the prescriber to change the order to an insulin glargine bolus, avoiding regular insulin altogether.

after.text: Administer the regular insulin dose immediately as ordered, then reassess the vial concentration afterward.
Recalculate the dose using the concentration of the insulin vial and draw the correct volume in the tuberculin syringe.
Assess the patient’s airway and breathing before administering the insulin dose.
Provide regular insulin for a patient with suspected adrenal insufficiency.

whyEachWrong.a: The dose is given before confirming the correct concentration, violating the required verification step.
whyEachWrong.c: Airway and breathing assessment is not the priority for insulin administration in this scenario.
whyEachWrong.d: Regular insulin is not the appropriate treatment for adrenal insufficiency.

stem: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation and a mechanical mitral valve is admitted for a lower extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT). He is started on a continuous intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion (target aPTT 60-80 seconds) and warfarin 5 mg daily. On hospital day 3, his labs are: PT/INR 2.6, aPTT 72 seconds, hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL (baseline 13.5 g/dL), platelets 210,000/µL, serum creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. He reports mild bruising at the infusion site but no overt bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in managing his anticoagulation regimen?

before.text: Decrease the heparin infusion rate to achieve a target aPTT of 50-60 seconds while maintaining the current warfarin dose
Hold the heparin infusion and continue warfarin alone, aiming for an INR of 2.5-3.5
Continue both heparin and warfarin at the current doses and recheck labs in 24 hours
Switch from unfractionated heparin to a weight-based low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) dose

after.text: Continue the heparin infusion and add warfarin, checking the aPTT in 12 hours.
Hold the heparin infusion and continue warfarin alone, aiming for an INR of 2.5-3.5
Increase the warfarin dose to reach an INR of 3.5 while maintaining the heparin infusion.
Hold the heparin and start low‑molecular‑weight heparin, aiming for an aPTT of 60‑80 seconds.

whyEachWrong.a: Action is appropriate but should be done after confirming INR stability, not immediately.
whyEachWrong.c: Correct adjustment of warfarin but not the priority; heparin should be stopped first.
whyEachWrong.d: Applies to a different anticoagulation scenario (e.g., LMWH for PE) rather than the current DVT case.

stem: A 45‑year‑old male construction worker is brought to the emergency department 45 minutes after a 30% total body surface area (TBSA) flame burn involving his anterior torso and both upper extremities. Initial vital signs are: BP 110/68 mmHg, HR 118/min, RR 24/min, Temp 37.8°C, SpO₂ 96% on room air. Laboratory studies reveal: Hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, Hematocrit 38%, Serum Na⁺ 138 mEq/L, Serum K⁺ 4.1 mEq/L, Serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, Serum lactate 2.8 mmol/L, and a base excess of –3.0 mEq/L. The trauma team initiates fluid resuscitation. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial fluid order for this patient?

before.text: Lactated Ringer's solution at 2 mL/kg per %TBSA burned over the first 24 hours
Lactated Ringer's solution at 4 mL/kg per %TBSA burned over the first 24 hours, with the first half given in the first 8 hours
Normal saline bolus of 20 mL/kg followed by lactated Ringer's at 3 mL/kg per %TBSA burned over 24 hours
Dextrose 5% in water at 4 mL/kg per %TBSA burned over 24 hours

after.text: Normal saline at 4 mL/kg per %TBSA burned over the first 24 hours, with the first half given after the initial 8‑hour period
Lactated Ringer's solution at 4 mL/kg per %TBSA burned over the first 24 hours, with the first half given in the first 8 hours
Lactated Ringer's solution at 4 mL/kg per %TBSA over 24 h, with the first half administered in the first 8 h, then place the patient on a cardiac monitor and order tetanus prophylaxis
Intravenous dopamine infusion titrated to maintain mean arterial pressure, initiated after confirming a serum lactate >4 mmol/L

whyEachWrong.a: Fluid should be started immediately; delaying the first half violates the recommended early resuscitation timing.
whyEachWrong.c: Although the fluid order matches the key, the added steps (cardiac monitoring and tetanus prophylaxis) are not the priority for initial burn resuscitation.
whyEachWrong.d: Dopamine is appropriate for hypotensive shock, not for the early fluid‑resuscitation phase of a burn patient with relatively stable blood pressure.

stem: A 28‑year‑old woman at 34 weeks gestation is admitted for severe preeclampsia with a blood pressure of 178/112 mmHg, headache, and visual disturbances. Laboratory studies reveal: serum magnesium 1.6 mg/dL (normal 1.7‑2.2 mg/dL), platelet count 110,000/µL, serum creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, and urine protein 3+. She is placed on continuous intravenous magnesium sulfate therapy per the Pritchard regimen (4 g IV loading dose, then 2 g IM in each buttock every 4 hours). After 6 hours, her serum magnesium rises to 3.8 mg/dL, and she develops diminished deep tendon reflexes, mild respiratory depression (respiratory rate 10/min), and a urine output of 25 mL/hr. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

before.text: Decrease the magnesium sulfate infusion rate to 1 g per hour
Discontinue the magnesium sulfate infusion and administer 40 mEq of calcium gluconate IV over 5 minutes
Continue the current magnesium sulfate regimen and initiate a dopamine infusion to improve urine output
Add a loop diuretic to increase magnesium excretion while maintaining the infusion

after.text: Administer 2 g of magnesium sulfate intramuscularly in each buttock now and continue the infusion.
Discontinue the magnesium sulfate infusion and administer 40 mEq of calcium gluconate IV over 5 minutes
Increase the magnesium sulfate infusion rate to achieve higher serum magnesium levels.
Begin an intravenous infusion of labetalol to control hypertension in severe preeclampsia.

whyEachWrong.a: Intervention should be performed after stopping the infusion, not before.
whyEachWrong.c: Managing magnesium toxicity takes precedence over adjusting magnesium dosage.
whyEachWrong.d: Labetalol treats hypertension, not magnesium toxicity, which is the current issue.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with a history of stage III ovarian cancer is admitted for chemotherapy. On postoperative day 3, she develops sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and tachypnea. Vital signs: BP 112/68 mmHg, HR 118/min, RR 28/min, SpO₂ 88% on room air. Physical exam reveals clear lungs, a faint systolic murmur at the left sternal border, and mild calf tenderness bilaterally. Laboratory results: D-dimer 2.4 µg/mL (reference <0.5), arterial blood gas on 2 L nasal cannula shows pH 7.46, PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, PaO₂ 62 mmHg. A bedside transthoracic echocardiogram shows right ventricular (RV) dilation with McConnell's sign. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

before.text: Initiate intravenous unfractionated heparin and arrange for immediate catheter-directed thrombolysis
Start therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin) and obtain a CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) when the patient is hemodynamically stable
Administer a weight-based bolus of alteplase (tPA) followed by continuous infusion
Begin oral rivaroxaban therapy without further imaging

after.text: Order a CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) and then start therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin) after imaging confirms the diagnosis
Start therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin) and obtain a CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) when the patient is hemodynamically stable
Apply high-flow oxygen therapy and monitor vital signs while awaiting definitive imaging
Start intravenous tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) for suspected massive myocardial infarction

whyEachWrong.a: Imaging should follow anticoagulation in a stable patient; ordering CTPA first delays treatment
whyEachWrong.c: Oxygen and monitoring are important but not the priority; anticoagulation is needed first
whyEachWrong.d: tPA is indicated for massive MI, not for pulmonary embolism in this stable patient

stem: A 68-year-old man with hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3 (baseline creatinine 1.5 mg/dL), and newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation (AF) is admitted for rate control and anticoagulation. He is hemodynamically stable (BP 132/78 mmHg, HR 98 bpm) and his labs show: Na 138 mEq/L, K 4.2 mEq/L, INR 1.1, and creatinine 1.5 mg/dL. The physician recommends initiating a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) for stroke prevention. During the discussion, the patient asks, “What are the risks if I don’t take the medication?” The physician explains that the drug reduces stroke risk by ~60% but carries a 2% risk of major bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage. The patient signs the consent form without further questions. Two days later, the patient suffers an ischemic stroke. The family files a complaint alleging that the patient was not adequately informed of the risks and benefits of the anticoagulation therapy. Which of the following actions by the nurse is most appropriate in response to the family’s complaint?

before.text: Explain that the physician provided all required information and that the patient’s decision was based on his own preferences.
Review the medical record to confirm that the informed consent discussion, including the risks of stroke and bleeding, was documented and then provide that documentation to the family.
Apologize to the family for the outcome and suggest that the physician should meet with them to discuss the case further.
Advise the family that the nurse is not involved in the consent process and therefore cannot comment on the adequacy of the consent.

after.text: Document the patient's vital signs and lab results before discussing the anticoagulation plan, then provide the documentation to the family later.
Review the medical record to confirm that the informed consent discussion, including the risks of stroke and bleeding, was documented and then provide that documentation to the family.
Explain the medication schedule to the patient and ensure he understands the dosing times before addressing the family complaint.
Review the cardiac monitor for arrhythmia episodes and provide that data to the family as evidence of proper care.

whyEachWrong.a: The action should occur before the family complaint, not after the discussion.
whyEachWrong.c: Addressing medication timing is not the priority over the informed consent issue.
whyEachWrong.d: Reviewing arrhythmia data pertains to a different condition, not the consent documentation.

stem: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of increased work of breathing over the past 12 hours. She was born at term via uncomplicated vaginal delivery. Her immunizations are up to date. On exam, she is irritable, has nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, and a grunting sound on expiration. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), heart rate 150/min, respiratory rate 58/min, blood pressure 85/55 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 88% on room air. A chest radiograph shows diffuse hyperinflation with peribronchial thickening. The infant's arterial blood gas on 2 L/min nasal cannula oxygen reveals pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 55 mmHg, PaO₂ 55 mmHg, and HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

before.text: Administer nebulized albuterol and start a course of oral azithromycin
Increase supplemental oxygen to 40% FiO₂ via a non-rebreather mask and obtain a pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) consult for possible intubation
Begin high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy at 2 L/kg/min and monitor respiratory status closely
Provide a dose of intramuscular epinephrine and order a rapid viral panel

after.text: Administer nebulized albuterol now and reassess respiratory status later
Obtain a chest CT scan to evaluate for possible pneumonia
Begin high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy at 2 L/kg/min and monitor respiratory status closely
Begin intravenous antibiotics for suspected bacterial sepsis

whyEachWrong.a: Intervention should be initiated after confirming need for HFNC, not before
whyEachWrong.b: Imaging is not the immediate priority; airway and breathing support precede diagnostics
whyEachWrong.d: Antibiotics target bacterial infection, not the viral bronchiolitis causing the current presentation

stem: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is admitted for treatment of community-acquired pneumonia. His home regimen includes basal insulin glargine 20 units nightly and rapid-acting insulin lispro 6 units with meals. On hospital day 2, his blood glucose values are: fasting 212 mg/dL, pre‑lunch 198 mg/dL, pre‑dinner 185 mg/dL, and bedtime 210 mg/dL. The attending orders a basal‑bolus regimen of insulin glargine 20 units subcutaneously at 2200 h and insulin lispro 4 units before each meal. The nurse prepares the lispro dose using a 1‑mL insulin syringe (U‑100) and draws up the dose from a vial labeled "Insulin Lispro 100 U/mL". Before administering the dose, the nurse notices the syringe is missing a label indicating the needle gauge. Which of the following actions is the most appropriate to ensure safe insulin administration?

before.text: Administer the insulin as prepared and document the missing needle gauge label as a minor incident.
Verify the needle gauge by checking the syringe barrel markings, confirm the dose, and then administer the insulin.
Discard the syringe, obtain a new syringe with a confirmed gauge, and prepare a fresh dose of insulin.
Call the pharmacy to request a pre‑filled insulin pen to avoid the need for syringe verification.

after.text: Administer the insulin dose immediately and verify the syringe gauge after the medication is given.
Check the patient's blood glucose level before addressing the missing syringe gauge issue.
Discard the syringe, obtain a new syringe with a confirmed gauge, and prepare a fresh dose of insulin.
Replace the syringe with a new one and draw up insulin for a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis.

whyEachWrong.a: Action is correct but performed before confirming syringe gauge, violating the correct sequence.
whyEachWrong.b: Blood glucose check is appropriate but not the priority over ensuring proper equipment.
whyEachWrong.d: Management is appropriate for diabetic ketoacidosis, not for the presented pneumonia case.

stem: A 68-year-old male with a history of hypertension and chronic kidney disease (stage 3) is admitted for acute decompensated heart failure. On admission his vitals are BP 158/92 mmHg, HR 112 bpm, RR 22 breaths/min, O2 sat 93% on 2 L nasal cannula. Labs show: Na 138 mEq/L, K 5.2 mEq/L, Cr 1.8 mg/dL, BUN 38 mg/dL, BNP 820 pg/mL. The attending orders a loop diuretic and requests a cardiology consult. The patient’s daughter calls the nursing unit and asks for a detailed explanation of the patient’s medication regimen and the cardiology team’s plan. The nurse knows the daughter is not listed as a health care proxy. According to HIPAA regulations, what is the most appropriate response by the nurse?

before.text: Provide the daughter with a full description of the medication orders and the cardiology consult plan, as she is a family member.
Explain that the nurse cannot discuss the patient’s specific medical information without the patient’s written authorization or a designated proxy.
Tell the daughter that the patient’s medication list is available on the hospital’s patient portal, which she can access with the patient’s login credentials.
Ask the patient if he consents to sharing his medical information with his daughter and, if he agrees, provide the details immediately.

after.text: Tell the daughter that you will discuss the plan with the patient and provide details after the physician’s order is completed.
Explain that the nurse cannot discuss the patient’s specific medical information without the patient’s written authorization or a designated proxy.
Explain the medication regimen and cardiology plan now, but also remind the daughter to schedule a follow‑up appointment.
Inform the daughter that the patient’s hypertension needs tighter control and suggest adjusting the antihypertensive medication.

whyEachWrong.a: The nurse should first verify authorization before any discussion, not after orders are completed.
whyEachWrong.c: Providing the information now violates privacy despite being helpful; the priority is confidentiality.
whyEachWrong.d: The information pertains to hypertension, not the acute heart failure scenario presented.

stem: A 68-year-old man with a history of ulcerative colitis is admitted for a severe flare requiring intravenous corticosteroids. On hospital day 3, he develops watery diarrhea (8 stools/day) and a fever of 38.9°C (102°F). Laboratory studies show a white blood cell count of 14,500/µL with 85% neutrophils and a serum creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL). Stool PCR is positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin B. The infection control team places the patient on contact precautions. Which of the following actions is the most critical component of preventing transmission of C. difficile in this setting?

before.text: Require all healthcare personnel to wear N95 respirators when entering the patient’s room
Perform hand hygiene with soap and water before and after patient contact, even if gloves are worn
Use a dedicated patient-care equipment cart that is not shared with other patients
Place the patient’s room under negative pressure ventilation to limit airborne spread

after.text: Administer oral metronidazole before performing hand hygiene with soap and water, then place gloves on the patient
Perform hand hygiene with soap and water before and after patient contact, even if gloves are worn
Place the patient in a private room and use contact precautions, but delay hand hygiene until the end of the shift
Perform hand hygiene with an alcohol-based sanitizer before and after patient contact, as you would for MRSA infection

whyEachWrong.a: Hand hygiene must be performed first; administering medication before it is out of sequence
whyEachWrong.c: Hand hygiene is the priority; delaying it makes it non‑essential despite isolation measures
whyEachWrong.d: Alcohol‑based sanitizer is ineffective against C. difficile spores; soap and water is required

stem: Mrs. Alvarez, a 72-year-old woman with Parkinson disease for 8 years, presents to the clinic for routine follow-up. She reports that her "off" periods have become more frequent, occurring 2–3 hours after her morning dose of carbidopa/levodopa (Sinemet) and lasting about 45 minutes before she takes her next dose. She takes Sinemet 25/100 mg (carbidopa 25 mg/levodopa 100 mg) three times daily at 07:00, 13:00, and 19:00. Her home blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg, heart rate 68/min, and weight is stable at 62 kg. Laboratory studies are within normal limits: serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, ALT 22 U/L, AST 19 U/L. She is not on any MAO-B inhibitors or COMT inhibitors. Which of the following medication timing adjustments is most likely to reduce her morning "off" episodes while maintaining safety?

before.text: Add a dose of carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 mg at 09:30, 2.5 hours after the morning dose.
Split the morning dose into two administrations of 12.5/50 mg each, given at 07:00 and 08:30.
Increase the morning dose to 37.5/150 mg and keep the dosing times unchanged.
Change the morning dose to an extended‑release formulation (carbidopa/levodopa ER 25/100 mg) given at 07:00.

after.text: Administer the full morning dose of 25/100 mg at 07:00, then repeat the same dose at 09:30.
Split the morning dose into two administrations of 12.5/50 mg each, given at 07:00 and 08:30.
Increase the morning dose to 30/120 mg at 07:00 while keeping the other doses unchanged.
Add a nighttime dose of 25/100 mg at 22:00 to address possible nocturnal Parkinson symptoms.

whyEachWrong.a: Provides the dose too early and repeats it later, which does not address the off period timing.
whyEachWrong.c: Higher dose may improve symptoms but is not the safest first step; timing adjustment is higher priority.
whyEachWrong.d: Targets nocturnal symptoms, not the morning off episodes described in the stem.

stem: A 68-year-old man with a history of severe COPD, atrial fibrillation, and recent stroke is admitted for acute respiratory failure. He is placed on high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) at 60 L/min, FiO₂ 0.6, and is receiving IV diltiazem for rate control. On day 2, his mental status deteriorates (GCS 10) and he becomes agitated, attempting to remove the HFNC cannula despite repeated verbal redirection. The nurse applies a soft wrist restraint to prevent self-extubation. Which of the following actions is the most appropriate next step to ensure restraint safety and prevent complications?

before.text: Leave the restraint in place for 24 hours and reassess the patient only if he becomes agitated again.
Check the patient's neurovascular status, skin integrity, and respiratory parameters every 2 hours, and document the need for continued restraint.
Apply a second, tighter restraint to the opposite wrist to further limit movement.
Remove the restraint immediately and initiate physical restraints on the torso instead.

after.text: Document the restraint and reassess the need after 24 hours, noting neurovascular status and skin integrity
Check the patient's neurovascular status, skin integrity, and respiratory parameters every 2 hours, and document the need for continued restraint.
Increase the FiO2 to 0.8 and administer a sedative to calm the patient before checking the restraint
Apply a soft ankle restraint and check peripheral pulses, assuming the patient has a lower extremity fracture

whyEachWrong.a: Restraint assessment should be done frequently, not delayed 24 hours
whyEachWrong.c: Addressing oxygenation and sedation precedes restraint safety in this scenario
whyEachWrong.d: Ankle restraint is for lower extremity issues, not appropriate for respiratory failure

stem: A 68‑year‑old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and severe osteoarthritis is admitted for a hip fracture repair. Postoperatively, he receives a patient‑controlled analgesia (PCA) pump delivering hydromorphone 0.2 mg per demand with a lockout interval of 6 minutes, and a background infusion of 0.5 mg/hour. Six hours after surgery, the nurse notes the patient is difficult to arouse, with a respiratory rate of 6 breaths/min, oxygen saturation of 82% on room air, and a capillary blood glucose of 112 mg/dL. His arterial blood gas shows pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 58 mmHg, PaO₂ 58 mmHg on 2 L nasal cannula. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

before.text: Increase the PCA lockout interval to 12 minutes and reduce the background infusion rate.
Immediately discontinue the PCA pump and administer naloxone intravenously.
Provide supplemental oxygen via non‑rebreather mask and obtain a repeat arterial blood gas in 30 minutes.
Administer intravenous flumazenil to reverse potential benzodiazepine co‑administration.

after.text: Administer oxygen via face mask and reassess respiratory status later
Immediately discontinue the PCA pump and administer naloxone intravenously.
Increase the background infusion rate of the PCA pump
Discontinue the PCA pump and administer naloxone for suspected myocardial infarction

whyEachWrong.a: Intervention is appropriate but should be done after securing the airway
whyEachWrong.c: Addressing analgesia does not address the immediate life‑threatening respiratory depression
whyEachWrong.d: Naloxone is indicated for opioid overdose, not for myocardial infarction

stem: During a night shift in a 45-bed medical-surgical unit, RN Alex receives an order from a locum physician, Dr. Patel, to administer 100 mg of intravenous (IV) haloperidol over 30 minutes to a 68-year-old patient with a recent diagnosis of sepsis, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease stage 3. The patient’s current vitals are: BP 92/58 mmHg, HR 112 bpm, RR 22/min, SpO₂ 94% on room air, and temperature 38.2°C (100.8°F). Recent labs show: serum creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (baseline 1.4 mg/dL), BUN 38 mg/dL, potassium 4.6 mEq/L, and a recent ECG demonstrates a QTc of 520 ms. The unit’s policy states that any order that appears unsafe must be clarified with the prescriber and, if unresolved, escalated through the chain of command. Which action should RN Alex take first?

before.text: Administer the haloperidol as ordered because the physician’s order supersedes unit policy.
Contact Dr. Patel to discuss the potential risks and request clarification or modification of the order.
Refuse to give the medication and document the refusal in the patient’s chart without further discussion.
Immediately notify the hospital’s risk management department before taking any further action.

after.text: Document the medication administration in the patient’s record and monitor vital signs after the infusion is completed.
Contact Dr. Patel to discuss the potential risks and request clarification or modification of the order.
Assess the patient’s pain level and provide a non‑pharmacologic comfort measure before addressing the medication order.
Administer a dose of intravenous furosemide to treat possible fluid overload, as the patient’s blood pressure is low.

whyEachWrong.a: The action should be taken before the medication is given, not after the infusion.
whyEachWrong.c: Pain assessment is appropriate but not the priority when an unsafe medication order is present.
whyEachWrong.d: Furosemide addresses fluid overload, not the safety concern of haloperidol with a prolonged QTc.

stem: A 34-year-old man is admitted to a medical‑surgical unit with a 3‑week history of productive cough, night sweats, and weight loss. His temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse 102/min, respirations 22/min, and blood pressure 118/74 mmHg. A sputum acid‑fast bacilli (AFB) smear returns positive. The infection control nurse orders airborne precautions. Which of the following actions is the most appropriate to ensure the effectiveness of these precautions for this patient?

before.text: Place the patient in a private room with the door closed and keep the window open for additional ventilation.
Place the patient in a negative‑pressure isolation room and ensure that the room’s air is exhausted directly to the outdoors.
Place the patient in a private room and use a portable HEPA filter unit to clean the air.
Place the patient in a private room and require staff to wear surgical masks when entering the room.

after.text: Place the patient on a surgical mask and educate on cough etiquette before moving to isolation.
Place the patient in a negative‑pressure isolation room and ensure that the room’s air is exhausted directly to the outdoors.
Administer the prescribed anti‑tuberculosis medication immediately after admission.
Place the patient in a negative‑pressure isolation room and ensure the room’s air is filtered through HEPA for a viral infection.

whyEachWrong.a: The action is appropriate but should be done after the patient is already in isolation, not before.
whyEachWrong.c: Treating the infection is important but does not ensure the effectiveness of airborne precautions, which is the priority.
whyEachWrong.d: HEPA filtration is used for certain viral infections, not for tuberculosis; the correct precaution for TB is exhaust to the outdoors.

stem: A 68-year-old man with a recent hospitalization for community‑acquired pneumonia presents to the emergency department with a 3‑day history of watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, and low-grade fever. His vitals are: temperature 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse 96/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, and SpO₂ 97% on room air. Laboratory studies show leukocytosis (WBC 14,500/mm³) with neutrophil predominance, serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL), and a stool PCR positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin B. The patient is placed in a private room. Which of the following additional infection‑control measures is the most appropriate to prevent transmission of C. difficile to other patients and healthcare workers?

before.text: Place the patient on airborne precautions and use a negative‑pressure isolation room.
Implement contact precautions with gown and glove use for all patient interactions and ensure environmental cleaning with sporicidal agents.
Require all staff to wear N95 respirators during patient care and limit visitors to one per day.
Apply droplet precautions, providing surgical masks to anyone entering the room.

after.text: Begin oral metronidazole therapy before initiating contact precautions and environmental cleaning.
Implement contact precautions with gown and glove use for all patient interactions and ensure environmental cleaning with sporicidal agents.
Place the patient on airborne isolation with a negative-pressure room and N95 respirator use.
Start intravenous vancomycin for presumed methicillin‑resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection and isolate the patient accordingly.

whyEachWrong.a: Infection control measures must precede antimicrobial therapy; the key principle is to implement contact precautions first.
whyEachWrong.c: C. difficile requires contact, not airborne, precautions; the priority principle is appropriate isolation type.
whyEachWrong.d: Vancomycin for MRSA addresses a different pathogen; the principle is that the measure must target C. difficile.

stem: A 62‑year‑old man with COPD is post‑operative day 3 after a total laryngectomy with a permanent tracheostomy. His temperature is 38.3°C (101°F), heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, and SpO₂ 94% on 2 L/min via tracheostomy collar. The tracheostomy tube is a size 8 cuffed tube with the cuff deflated. On inspection, there is thin, serosanguineous drainage around the stoma, and the inner cannula is noted to be moist with pink secretions. The nurse reports that the patient has been coughing up thick secretions and has difficulty clearing them. A chest X‑ray shows mild bibasilar infiltrates. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in tracheostomy care?

before.text: Increase the FiO₂ to 0.5 and place the patient on continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) via the tracheostomy.
Perform a sterile inner cannula change, suction the airway with a size‑12 French catheter, and instill normal saline as needed.
Apply a humidified oxygen hood over the stoma and order a bronchoscopy to evaluate for granulation tissue.
Replace the cuffed tracheostomy tube with a larger (size 9) cuffed tube and inflate the cuff to prevent aspiration.

after.text: Change the inner cannula using sterile technique, then suction with a size‑12 French catheter, postponing any saline flush.
Perform a sterile inner cannula change, suction the airway with a size‑12 French catheter, and instill normal saline as needed.
Administer broad‑spectrum antibiotics, monitor vitals, and continue routine tracheostomy care.
Replace the cuffed tube with a larger uncuffed tube and start humidified oxygen therapy.

whyEachWrong.a: Saline should be instilled immediately; delaying it makes the sequence incorrect.
whyEachWrong.c: Antibiotics are not the priority; airway clearance precedes infection management.
whyEachWrong.d: Tube replacement addresses tube obstruction, not the current infection and secretion issue.

stem: A 68-year-old male with a history of severe COPD, atrial fibrillation on warfarin, and recent right middle cerebral artery stroke is admitted to the medical-surgical unit for acute exacerbation of COPD. On admission his vitals are: T 37.2°C, HR 112 bpm (irregularly irregular), RR 28 breaths/min, BP 138/82 mmHg, SpO2 88% on 2 L nasal cannula. He is placed on BiPAP (IPAP 12 cm H2O, EPAP 6 cm H2O) and started on IV methylprednisolone, nebulized albuterol/ipratropium, and prophylactic subcutaneous heparin. Over the next 2 hours his respiratory status deteriorates, and he becomes agitated, attempting to remove the BiPAP mask and pull out his IV line. The nurse assesses his mental status as disoriented to person and place, but able to follow simple commands. The physician orders a soft wrist restraint to prevent device removal while continuing noninvasive ventilation. Which of the following actions is the MOST appropriate to ensure restraint safety for this patient?

before.text: Apply the soft wrist restraint and document the order; reassess the patient’s mental status every 30 minutes.
Apply the soft wrist restraint, ensure a second qualified staff member is present at all times, and perform a full neurovascular assessment of the restrained limb every hour.
Apply the soft wrist restraint, place the patient in a supine position, and increase the BiPAP pressure to improve ventilation.
Apply the soft wrist restraint, document the order, and schedule a physician reassessment in 4 hours.

after.text: Apply the soft wrist restraint after the patient has been calmized and the BiPAP settings have been adjusted, then document the intervention.
Apply the soft wrist restraint, ensure a second qualified staff member is present at all times, and perform a full neurovascular assessment of the restrained limb every hour.
Apply the soft wrist restraint, ensure a second qualified staff member is present, and administer a dose of IV lorazepam to reduce agitation.
Apply the soft wrist restraint, ensure a second qualified staff member is present, and obtain a chest CT to evaluate for possible pneumothorax before proceeding.

whyEachWrong.a: The restraint should be applied immediately to prevent device removal, not delayed until after calming or adjusting settings.
whyEachWrong.c: The priority is to maintain airway and ventilation; adding sedation is not the immediate safety focus.
whyEachWrong.d: Obtaining a chest CT addresses a respiratory complication, not the stroke-related neurovascular assessment required for this patient.

stem: A 62-year-old man with metastatic colorectal cancer is admitted for sepsis secondary to a urinary tract infection. He is intubated and transferred to the ICU.
